title: Bernard Lown and engineer Barouh Berkovits developed a direct-current shock that returns the heart to a normal rhythm

trailer.text: Dr. Bernard Lown, a Harvard cardiologist, was one of the founders of IPPNW, the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on behalf of the organization.
Dr. Bernard Lown was a Harvard cardiologist, a Jew born in Lithuania, who left his native country with his family to escape Nazi persecution.
Before the 1960s, little could be done to prevent sudden death from arrhythmias, and the alternating current used to try to help the heart could injure it and even kill.
Lown administered shocks through the chest walls of 11 patients, some near death, and restored a normal rhythm to all of them.
According to the New York Times, it was the first effective defibrillator, and by 1964 thousands of hospitals were equipped with it.

glance.label: Recognition
glance.value: Nobel Peace Prize, on behalf of IPPNW

paragraphs.text: Bernard Lown was born on June 7, 1921, in Utena, Lithuania, to his parents Nisson and Bella.
According to the New York Times, one of his grandfathers was a rabbi in Lithuania.
The Jewish family left Lithuania to escape Nazi persecution.
Lown said that some members of his family were killed in the Holocaust.
In 1935 the family emigrated to Maine, and his father ran a shoe factory there, in Pittsfield.
Lown said that he came to the United States as a boy.
In 1942 he received a bachelor's degree from the University of Maine, and in 1945 a medical degree from Johns Hopkins.
At Johns Hopkins he was suspended from his studies because he organized a lecture by a Black physician on health in the Black community.
He then trained in cardiology at the Brigham hospital, under the mentorship of Dr. Samuel Levine.
During the McCarthy era he was drafted for the Korean War, discharged, and redrafted as a private after he refused to name organizations he had worked with for peace and social justice.
Myocardial infarction patients were then kept on strict bed rest for several weeks, and this regimen carried a mortality rate of up to 35%.
In 1952 Lown and Levine recommended in JAMA that patients rest in an armchair, not in bed.
They got patients up in a chair as early as the second day, to the resentment of other physicians.
According to the Life in the Fast Lane website, the chair treatment greatly shortened the length of hospital stay and reduced early mortality by two-thirds.

stations.title: Direct current, at the right moment

paragraphs.text: Before the 1960s, little could be done to prevent sudden death from arrhythmias, and patients were kept in bed for weeks.
At the time, fibrillations were believed to be responsible for 40 percent of the half-million fatal heart attacks in the United States every year.
According to the New York Times, earlier attempts with alternating current were too imprecise to avoid the vulnerable points in the heart's cycle, and often ended in death.
According to the Carnegie Corporation, Lown wondered why an early alternating-current defibrillator had failed to save one of his patients.
He found that alternating current could injure the heart and even cause death.
In 1959, in animal experiments, the two found that alternating current caused burns to skeletal muscle and heart muscle.
According to NYU Tandon, Berkovits conceived the idea that direct current would be safer and more effective.
In 1961 Lown found that a specific direct-current waveform stopped ventricular fibrillation and restored a normal rhythm, without injuring the heart or skeletal muscle.
A short electrical discharge was timed to be given outside the vulnerable period on the electrocardiogram, and in this way ventricular fibrillation was avoided.
Lown found that ventricular fibrillation was 10 times more frequent after alternating-current cardioversion than after direct-current cardioversion.
According to NYU Tandon, the two men's joint work produced a patent in 1962.

stations.title: From 11 patients to hospitals around the world

paragraphs.text: Lown administered shocks through the chest walls of 11 patients, some near death, and restored a normal rhythm to all of them.
According to the Life in the Fast Lane website, this was the first machine used successfully on humans at Brigham Hospital.
In 1962 Lown published the experiments in a report to the American Society for Clinical Investigation.
The device was manufactured by American Optical, and by 1964 thousands of hospitals were equipped with it.
According to the New York Times, the breakthrough became a lifesaving technique worldwide and helped make open-heart surgery possible.
It opened an era of resuscitation techniques, among them modern pacemakers and implanted defibrillators.
According to Harvard University, the cardioverter has saved many lives around the world.
Former Vice President Dick Cheney, who suffered from heart disease for decades and had a pacemaker and defibrillator implanted in 2001, is probably the most prominent beneficiary of this advance.

stations.title: More ways to keep the rhythm

paragraphs.text: At the Brigham hospital in Boston, Lown organized one of the first coronary care units, which focused on preventing heart rhythm disorders.
Lown and others realized that nurses could be just as competent in using lidocaine and even in defibrillation.
Lown demonstrated the critical role of potassium in reducing the risk of digitalis toxicity.
In 1973 he reported that sleep was better than many potent cardiac drugs in controlling dangerous heart rhythms.
Lown said that Philip Noel-Baker taught him that the real death threat in the world was not cardiac, but nuclear.
He co-founded Physicians for Social Responsibility, to organize American physicians against the threat of nuclear war.
In 1980 seven American and Soviet physicians, including Lown, founded IPPNW, the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War.
In 1982, 100 million Soviet viewers heard for the first time an unedited discussion of the consequences of nuclear war.
Lown and Chazov, the organization's co-presidents, met with Mikhail Gorbachev.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee said that the organization had performed a considerable service to mankind by spreading authoritative information and by creating awareness of the catastrophic consequences of atomic warfare.
Lown and Chazov received the prize in Oslo on behalf of the organization.
On the eve of the Nobel Peace Prize award, a Russian journalist collapsed from cardiac arrest at a press conference, and Lown and Chazov helped resuscitate him and save his life.

stations.title: A satellite, a bridge and 99 years

paragraphs.text: According to the New York Times, Lown founded SatelLife USA, which in 1991 launched a communications satellite to help provide medical training and information to thousands of doctors in Africa and Asia.
Joseph Brain said that Lown persuaded the Soviet Union to repurpose a ballistic missile and launch his device.
In 1997, ProCor was founded to help doctors in developing countries.
In 2008 the Lown Scholars program was established at Harvard to train scientists and public health professionals from Africa, Asia and Latin America.
A bridge between Lewiston and Auburn is named after him: the Bernard Lown Peace Bridge.
Lown received 21 honorary degrees from universities in the United States and abroad.
In a 2008 interview he said that he wanted to be wrong, because by being wrong he learns how to be right.
Lown and his wife Louise were married for 73 years, and she died in 2019.
Lown died on February 16, 2021, at his home in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts, at the age of 99.
According to his granddaughter, he suffered from complications of heart failure and contracted pneumonia.
Conservative Western critics called IPPNW's leaders naïve, and argued that the organization's work served Soviet propaganda.
The prize was considered especially controversial because Chazov was the personal physician of the Kremlin leaders and had previously spoken out against Andrei Sakharov.

claims.text: לפי אתר Life in the Fast Lane, לאון קיבל ב-1942 תואר ראשון בקלאסיקה מאוניברסיטת מיין.
claims.quote: 1942 – B.A. (summa cum laude) in the classics from the University of Maine

claims.text: לפי אתר Life in the Fast Lane, לאון הוא מפתח הדפיברילטור בזרם ישר והקרדיוורטר (1961).
claims.quote: The original developer of the DC defibrillator and the cardioverter (1961)

claims.text: לפי PA, לאון המציא ב-1962 את הדפיברילטור בזרם ישר, הקרדיוורטר, המשתמש בהלם חשמלי כדי להחזיר את הלב לפעום.
claims.quote: In 1962, Dr Lown invented the direct-current defibrillator, or cardioverter, which uses electric shocks to get hearts to resume beating.

claims.text: לפי מכון לאון, המחקר של לאון אתגר את הנוהג להשכיב חולי התקף לב במיטה 4-6 שבועות.
claims.quote: challenging the conventional wisdom of keeping heart attack patients on bed rest for 4-6 weeks

claims.text: לפי PA, לאון הקים את 'רופאים לאחריות חברתית' ב-1960.
claims.quote: founding Physicians for Social Responsibility in 1960 and later co-founding International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War in the 1980s

claims.text: לפי ה-New York Times, עד 1985 הארגון אסף 135,000 חברים ב-41 מדינות.
claims.quote: the group had gathered 135,000 members in 41 countries by 1985, when it won the peace prize.

claims.text: לפי PA, בשיאו היו לארגון יותר מ-200,000 חברים וסניפים ביותר מ-60 מדינות.
claims.quote: At its peak, the group had more than 200,000 members and chapters in more than 60 countries.

claims.text: לפי אתר Life in the Fast Lane, לאון הקים את SATELLIFE ב-1987.
claims.quote: 1987 – Founded ‘SATELLIFE’ to provide health workers in developing nations free information services through satellite and Internet technologies
